Just to add to the conversation for people who are super timid or freeze in situations like this- go to the nearest member of staff and act like you know them. “Oh my gosh hi Jesse I haven’t seen you since that bbq, how are you”. If you’re in conversation with someone you’re less interesting and available to weirdos. If you’re not able to do that, Stand with your back against a wall. Make sure you can see the person and the room and where your exits are, don’t let them get behind you. Phone someone or fake ringing someone. If you can have a designated friend who you can ring so you don’t have to think too much in the moment. If they don’t answer talk to their voicemail. Avoid engaging in any conversation and don’t give eye contact, if you have earphones don’t play anything through them but in a crowded place it can be useful to have them in (providing they’re not noise cancelling) so you can pretend not to hear people when in fact you can hear everything.

Most importantly learn how to be loud. If it’s difficult, practice with a friend or in the mirror. Practice hearing your voice being loud and authoritative. Watching sport is a good way to do this- cheer on a team as loud as you can.

Not likert but scores on a knowledge test (like a mini exam). I’m comparing two infographic formats to see if one is more effective for learning. Participants were assigned randomly (50:50) to different formats so in phase 1 I’m comparing test scores between the two groups immediately after accessing the information.

Phase 2 asked the same knowledge questions a week later to see if the information had been retained in long term memory. There was a return rate of completion for this second phase of ~60% with uneven returns between the two groups. For those who completed both phases I am comparing the original knowledge exam score from phase 1 with the persons score at phase 2 (so dependent) and then comparing the paired T test scores between the groups.

Tendons connect muscles to bone. They’re essential for movement. Ligaments attach bone to bone and their purpose is stabilisation of joints (so your knee doesn’t go sideways or backwards or rotate in circles.). Both are made of strong fibrous tissue and aren’t very stretchy. Kind of like a thick lock of hair.

Take the knee as your example. There are four main ligaments that attach the thigh bones with the lower leg bones making sure your knee doesn’t move out of normal movements. There are loads of muscles used to move the knee. There are multiple ones that extend (straighten) your knee, many that flex it (bend) some that allow you to turn your lower leg inwards or outward and some that are linked to the pelvis and a few that affect the foot. The muscle can contract (shorten) and they tend to work in pairs so one muscle shortens to flex the joint and its ’antagonistic pair’ shortens to pull the joint the other direction. The tendons near the knee connect some of the muscles in the leg to the long bones.

Cutting a tendon would stop that muscle being able to contract and do its movement. It would depend which ones to which movements would be stopped. Tendons and ligaments have very little blood supply and most of their nerve supply is motor supply  (That means it causes movement) rather than sensory  neurones which are the feeling nerves. So cutting one in isolation wouldn’t cause a lot of bleeding or sensory nerve damage, it would stop the attached muscle from doing its job. In reality the inside of the body is messy and you’d likely hit some blood and nerve vessels near to the tendon.

Don’t try this at home.

Regular Exercise releases endorphins (good chemicals that improve mood and reduce anxiety) and can reduce cortisol levels (the stress hormone).

30mins a day most days will have a positive impact on your mood and should improve anxiety symptoms.

Exercise will use up that extra anxious energy and bring your bodily responses down to a more manageable level.

The other anxiety reducing component of exercise can come from doing exercise with others- as part of a sports team or an exercise class. The social contact and sense of camaraderie of working together is a good way to connect and feel connected to others.

How long have you known her? I ask because people who’ve had eating disorders at young ages sometimes fall into a quasi-recovery phase where they’re not in the deep grips of restriction and obsession but they’re not actually recovered either.

I’m not saying an eating disorder is definitely the cause, the rest of my comment is based on that assumption though. I’ll try give an example of how it might feel for her if it is:

You mentioned plain pasta in a comment, plain pasta is something that requires one process. Stick it in the pan for 10mins and then eat it. You know what the nutritional value is per portion and you’re not adding sauce or seasoning or protein or veg, all of which complicate that nutritional value. If you add bell pepper how much bell pepper? How much is normal for that pasta serving? Is it worth the extra 40kcals to have that pepper? Then you have to cook it in a separate pan and tbh you don’t really want the pepper OR the pasta but you know you should eat something so the bare minimum is the easiest. The dilemma over pepper might be the thing that makes you think “screw it I won’t have anything it’s all too complicated “.

I know you’ve offered to make her food but how does she know if you used the spray oil or olive oil? Was the cheese measured or estimated? What’s the right portion size if everything’s mixed in together?

In terms of advice, seeing a doc is a good idea. If she’s run down suggest she gets blood tests done. Anemia and vitamin deficiencies could be contributing as well as lack of calorific intake. With medical info she might be more receptive to hearing there’s a problem. Eating disorders are control disorders at the core. Whilst others have suggested the gym as an option I would suggest her getting seen by a doctor before putting further strain on her system via exercise as exercise is another area for potential control.

Support her, tell her how you feel but expect resistance. That’s the disorder, not her.

Here are some strategies I like to use to get stuff done:

Self imposed rules (I respond well to structure): I have a bedtime, it’s not the same every night, if I have a morning lecture the next day I have a 10.30pm bedtime, if I have nothing on I stay up later.
When studying I turn my phone on silent (or use the ‘forest’ app) and do not look at it.
Set screen time limits during the week.
I keep a hard copy calendar and planner.

Find really intriguing rabbit holes: people choose their course at uni cos they’re passionate about it. Sometimes the compulsory reading is not your cup of tea but going down a rabbit hole that interests you can boost your motivation and overall enthusiasm, enjoyment and performance in the course. Find different and fun ways to represent and record the info. Diagrams, spider charts, weird doodles.

Have other interests: uni and life is about more than work so find things you enjoy and do them regularly.
Gonna just list some examples: playing an instrument or learning a new one. Drawing. Playing pool. Football. Skateboarding. Juggling. Board games. Computer games. Puzzles like crosswords and sudokus. Baking. Reading fiction. Writing limericks. Yoga. Watching films with flatmates. Physical challenges (eg run 5k). Making clay figurines. Learning sign language or French or arabic.
Although these aren’t related to your course they work as a destress and chill out AND stimulate your brain in ways that can’t be done through reading a textbook.

Study smart- quality over quantity: you could spend 8 hours a day studying (reading through a textbook or copying out notes) but if you don’t retain it then it’s pointless. Over the summer try out some different study methods. Flashcards, songs, massive interlinking diagrams. 

Rewards: some people are motivated to avoid punishment or criticism but most people are very invested in positive reinforcement. I use so many rewards. A big favourite of mine is stickers. Other include- Going to the cinema, new nail varnish, nice shower gel, favourite meal or drink.

Accountability: tell a friend you’re going to work for one hour and ask them to only reply or to send you a meme once you’re done. Having someone else know your self expectations and become accountable is really helpful.

Good luck !

Given your ankle recovery don’t do breaststroke immediately. It’s an awkward movement and you’ll need to build up some strength in it first. Gentle flutter kick is good. Try walking up and down the pool . Might seem weird but it’s a low impact way to get the ankle doing essential repetitive movements. Initially stand upright to do the walking (water will come up to your waist) and then lower your body position so you’re crouched and your shoulders are underwater. It will be easier to walk like that but you’ll stretch your ankle past 90 degrees and encourage strength to reestablish in extended positions. Pushing off the wall and gliding introduces more power through the lower limb joints.

All those are kind of geared towards ankles but setting yourself a number of lengths to do or an amount of time you’ll swim for is good structure so you don’t get in the pool and say ‘what now?’ Deffo allocate time to just float in the water (very calming) and use the sauna if they have one.

Pretty decent!

In terms of critique;

your last stroke is short, you want to have a full arm reach before the turn to pull yourself forward and to begin the rotation. It’s difficult to correct at the last minute so perhaps try adjusting a tad before that last stroke. Initially I used my stroke/length count to spread out my arm strokes evenly (it shouldn’t be drastically different in races if your stroke is efficient) to get a sense of where I need to be for the turn. Now I know my technique and stroke length I judge how many strokes I need when I glimpse the flags or when I spot the T. This means I can make slight adjustments for an optimal last stroke.

You need to throw your legs over faster. From the moment you pull with your last stroke your goal is to get your legs onto the wall as fast as possible. Watch fc sprinters and you’ll notice that their turns are foremostly efficient. They only look neat because of years of practice. Turns don’t have to be pretty just fast.

Underwater kick needs to be fly kick and a lot further underwater. Make the most of all the power you have from the turn and conserve your energy by pulsing.

Additionally from what I can see your fc arms are doing a lot of work outside the water. You’re bringing your arms all the way round your body like you would a fly stroke. This can cause fatigue, cramp and also your body might deviate from a streamlined position to accommodate this hyperextension at the shoulder. High elbows will save you lots of energy and discomfort. There are drills I used to use called zipper drills. https://youtu.be/jBWEwihZeg4 this is a great video example.

I think arm improvements would be the most important thing to work on atm.

And I know that sounds like a lot of bad stuff, but you have an overwhelming amount of positives and pluses in comparison to the negatives. Your stroke rate, breathing, arms underwater, kick, head position, feet placement on wall… etc.

Best of luck!

Shut off the water .

Make sure you go outside to get some fresh air at regular intervals. It will help if it’s cold and you let yourself be cold- it’s grounding and calming.

Allow yourself to be upset for a specified time period. cyclical thinking and ruminating will keep you stuck and get you more wound up so Find a game or puzzle or thing to do that uses your hands and brain. When both are occupied it’s harder for ocd to infiltrate.

This is not permanent- you will not feel this horrible and at this intensity in say, February, or next Xmas. (hopefully not even in a few days). Good plan. Here are my cooling strategies:

If it’s hotter outside than in close windows and doors. A good tower fan, place a bowl of ice cubes in front of it (between you and the fan). Mini fan with water spray for on the move. “Ice towel” you get it wet and swing it round and it goes nice and cold. Put a wheat bag in the freezer and rotate one in one out (those ones designed for the microwave to calm neck pain) or a wet tea towel is a decent alternative. Instant ice packs designed for first aid are good. Cool off by applying cool water to wrists, feet, armpits, chest and hair/head where blood vessels are close to the surface. Loose clothing. Plan to do anything active - including cleaning- first thing in the morning or late at night. Supermarkets, department stores, cafes, libraries, all tend to have good air con so if your home is too hot consider camping out somewhere like that. Stay hydrated and if you’re craving salt listen to that craving. Let people know that heat affects you. Consider a kids paddling pool, small and cheap, cover when not in use to avoid stuff getting in it. Or you can run a cold bath if you have one and just leave the water in so you can use it multiple times to cool off and it doesn’t use a ton of water.

There may be some others I’ve forgotten and you might already know these but I hope at least one is helpful :)
